Western school whiting (Sillago vittata) exhibits typical life-history traits for a small, iteroparous marine teleost. Field studies conducted off the coast of Western Australia have documented that newly hatched individuals, emerging from pelagic eggs of approximately 0.66 mm in diameter, possess a minuscule wet weight at birth of only 0.00015 grams [Wwb = 0.00015 grams]. The age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation to chorion rupture, occurs approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] after spawning under a stable water temperature regime of 22.8 °C [T = 22.8 °C]. This brief yolk-dependent phase, characteristic of the lecithotrophic prolarva, is followed by the onset of exogenous feeding once the yolk sac is fully resorbed. The embryonic development period is relatively rapid compared to other sillaginids, likely reflecting an adaptive response to the warm, nutrient-poor waters of its shallow coastal habitat. Early-stage larvae are entirely reliant on endogenous reserves before transitioning to a diet of small copepod nauplii.

Sexual maturation in Sillago vittata is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body length, with individuals typically reaching puberty at a fork length of approximately 16 centimeters [Lp = approximately 16 centimeters]. This milestone represents the onset of gonad maturation and gametogenesis activation, marking the transition from a juvenile, immature teleost to a reproductively viable adult. Morphometric analyses of gonadal tissue indicate that vitellogenesis begins shortly after this size threshold is crossed. The ultimate fork length for the species, representing the maximum size recorded in wild adult populations, is 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is broadly consistent with the maximum recorded longevity and the observed growth trajectory, which follows a standard von Bertalanffy pattern. Compared to congeneric species such as Sillago sihama, Sillago vittata attains a slightly smaller maximum length, suggesting a relatively compressed growth period during adulthood.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified through direct gonadal examinations of gravid fish captured during the austral summer spawning season. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 22.8 °C [T = 22.8 °C], spawning females produce a remarkable fecundity of approximately 150,000 oocytes per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 150,000 oocytes per reproductive event], with an estimated frequency of approximately one spawning event each year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event each year]. This annual reproductive rhythm, characterised by a single prolonged spawning pulse, aligns with the seasonal availability of planktonic prey for the exogenously feeding pelagic larvae. Fecundity is positively correlated with female body size, with larger, older individuals contributing disproportionately more oocytes to the annual cohort. The high fecundity is a classic life-history adaptation to high larval mortality in the planktonic environment, where survivorship from the preflexion larva through metamorphosis is extremely low.

The maximum body mass attained by adult Sillago vittata has been estimated from length-weight regressions applied to field-caught specimens. The ultimate wet weight for the species, derived from the relationship 0.00851 multiplied by fork length raised to the power of 3.07, is 291.5 grams [Wwi = 291.5 grams]. This value is markedly lower than the adult masses reported for larger-bodied sillaginids, reflecting the slender, elongate body plan of this coastal whiting. The weight-length relationship is strongly allometric, indicating that weight increases more rapidly than the cube of length, a pattern commonly associated with deep-bodied or heavy-set fish. Condition factor indices calculated from these data suggest that adults in good nutritional status maintain relatively high somatic reserves prior to the spawning season. This pre-reproductive mass gain is essential for fuelling the energetically costly processes of gonadal recrudescence and the downstream investment in egg and spermatozoa production. Post-spawning, many individuals exhibit a noticeable decline in body condition.

Longevity records for Western school whiting, based on scale-reading and otolith increment analysis of wild populations maintained at 22.8 °C [T = 22.8 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan extends to approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days]. This maximum recorded longevity of roughly eight years places Sillago vittata among the longer-lived members of the genus, with most congeneric species rarely exceeding five to six years. The age distribution in sampled populations typically shows a strong bias toward younger age classes, with relatively few individuals surviving beyond their sixth year, a pattern attributable to natural mortality from piscivorous predators. The species exhibits a gradual senescence trajectory rather than a dramatic post-reproductive decline, with many older females continuing to produce viable oocytes until their terminal year. This extended reproductive window, combined with high annual fecundity, suggests a bet-hedging life-history strategy that buffers against stochastic environmental fluctuations in the shallow coastal ecosystems they inhabit.
